summary.title: Equity 101 for Software Engineers at Big Tech and Startups
summary.one_liner: You learn how equity compensation works for software engineers (stock options, RSUs, double-trigger RSUs, vesting, cliffs, and exercise windows) and which terms to check in an offer.
keywords: is equity worth it at tech companies
takeaways: Stock options give the right to buy shares at a strike price after vesting; they are worth something only if the exit price is above the strike price, and can be worthless (underwater) otherwise.

RSUs at public companies are awarded as shares or as a dollar value converted at vesting; double-trigger RSUs delay taxable vesting until an IPO or other liquidity event, to avoid paying tax on illiquid private stock.

Key terms to check: vesting period (4 years is standard), cliff (one year is typical at private companies), refreshers, clawbacks, and the post-termination exercise window (90 days is common; 10 years is better).
Exercising options costs money and may trigger tax, which can be very large at high-growth startups, so the exercise window and financing options matter.
Red flags include clawbacks on equity, vesting longer than 4 years, short exercise windows, and dollar-denominated stock grants in high-growth pre-IPO companies.
summary.summary: Gergely Orosz explains the most common equity compensation types offered by Big Tech and startups, including stock options (ESOPs and NSOs), RSUs, double-trigger RSUs, and a list of further terms such as phantom shares, SARs, and growth shares. He covers vesting, cliffs, refreshers, clawbacks, and exercise windows, with worked examples of gains and losses. The article also lists questions to ask when evaluating an offer and red flags to watch for. It is written as a high-level overview and explicitly not tax or legal advice.
